What is a transactional email service? A transactional email service delivers one-to-one messages triggered by a user action, such as password resets, magic links, order receipts, shipping alerts, and billing notifications. Your application triggers the send when an event happens, and Bird handles domain authentication, inbox delivery, bounce suppression, and real-time status tracking. Audience broadcasts and promotional newsletters belong in Email marketing. Should I send transactional email with SMTP or the Email API? Use SMTP to connect an existing application or framework mailer by swapping credentials without rewriting your sending code. Use the Email API when you want to populate published templates with dynamic data, prevent duplicate sends on network retries, and build with Bird’s SDKs, CLI, or MCP. Both share the same verified domains, suppression lists, webhooks, and delivery logs. Does a delivered transactional email mean it reached the inbox? A delivered status confirms that the recipient’s mail server accepted the message, though the mailbox provider still decides whether to place it in the primary inbox, promotions tab, or spam folder. Pair delivery logs with domain authentication and Inbox Insights to monitor inbox versus spam placement across major mailbox providers. Scale without losing control. We sign the message with DKIM, deliver it, and report each recipient's outcome. To send something before reading further, the quickstart takes you from an API key to a delivered message. This page covers the model the rest of this section assumes, and points at the guide for each part of it. How sending works A send is accepted in one call and delivered asynchronously. POST /v1/email/messages validates the payload and sending domain, then returns 202 Accepted with an em_ message ID. Read each recipient's outcome through webhook events or the message endpoints. Sending email covers the payload, field limits, and response. Two consequences of that model shape the rest of this section. One message, many recipients, one lifecycle each. A message to five addresses produces five independent outcomes, and the message-level status you read back is an aggregate over them. Suppression is evaluated the same way: one suppressed address comes back rejected while the other four deliver. Every message declares why you are sending it. A category of transactional or marketing decides which suppressions apply to it. Someone who unsubscribed from your newsletter still needs their password reset to arrive, and the category is what tells us the difference. A send can also arrive by another route, or leave later. SMTP accepts submissions from anything that speaks the protocol, and scheduled sending holds a message until a time you set. Where each guide fits Sending. Sending email is the one to read first: it owns the payload every other send path is a variation on. From there, templates store content you reuse, attachments add files, batch sending submits up to 100 messages in one request, and broadcasts send one email to a whole audience. Domains and authentication. Sending domains covers registering a domain and getting it verified. DKIM, SPF, and DMARC explains what each record proves to a receiving mailbox provider, and BIMI shows your logo beside your messages in email apps that support it. Reputation. Suppressions is the list of addresses we stop sending to, filled automatically from hard bounces and complaints; unsubscribes stop delivery the same way but through a stated preference instead of a suppression record. Dedicated IPs and pools and IP warmup cover sending from IP addresses only your organization uses. Email deliverability ties those together. Knowing what happened. The email log shows one message and its per-recipient timeline. Email metrics aggregates your traffic. Events is the event vocabulary and how webhooks deliver it to your own endpoint. Receiving. Receiving email covers both ways in: a forwarding address we generate that needs no DNS, or MX records on a subdomain you own. Agent mailboxes builds on that with inboxes your code sends from as well as reads. Testing. The mail sandbox exercises your integration end to end without delivering anywhere. Send to bounce@messagebird.dev to generate a hard bounce through the real event and webhook pipeline. The test writes nothing to your suppression list.
